analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes on large inheritances.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax was introduced on the first day of the 115th Congress with 61 Republican cosponsors, but it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax — the taxes paid when very large amounts of wealth are passed between generations. Only estates above a multi-million-dollar exemption owe the estate tax, so repeal would cut taxes for the heirs of the largest estates while removing that revenue from the Treasury. The bill never moved beyond its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — generally multimillion-dollar and billion-dollar family fortunes — would owe no federal tax on inherited wealth, and wealthy families would also avoid the gift tax when transferring money during life.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes [S3].
The repeal applies to estates of people dying, gifts made, and generation-skipping transfers made after enactment, so the largest inheritances would pass untaxed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and ultimately other taxpayers — would bear the cost, since the estate tax's revenue would disappear while the largest estates are exempted from tax on inherited wealth.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate all federal tax on very large inheritances, concentrating the benefit among the heirs of the wealthiest families and removing revenue that would otherwise come primarily from multimillion-dollar estates.
Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes removes all three transfer taxes at once, which would shrink federal revenue with no offset in the bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: only the largest estates owe the estate tax, so repeal mainly cuts taxes for very wealthy families, while the cost is the lost revenue that funds programs all taxpayers rely on. The bill contains no replacement for the revenue it removes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act of 2017 on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress [S1].
The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
Sixty-one Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
After the referral, no further action appears in the bill's record — no committee markup, no House vote, and no Senate action — so the bill died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax remained in place, preserving federal revenue that comes primarily from the largest estates and sparing other taxpayers from making up the difference. Wealthy families who supported repeal did not get it.

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the estate tax repeal on the first day of the 115th Congress.

for.name: 61 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 61 cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or a vote after its referral; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 61 cosponsors was a Republican, with no Democratic support in the record [S4].

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and wealthy families
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate federal tax on multimillion-dollar and billion-dollar inheritances; the estate tax applies only to estates above a large exemption, so the benefit concentrates at the top while the lost revenue falls on the general Treasury.
Repeal would shrink demand for estate-tax avoidance planning while easing rules for transferring wealth; the effect is modest either way.
